title: US bird species followed route land-cover change at 11-25% of spatial predictions, about twice their temperature transfer, and land-cover change did not slow community warming (BBS, LCMAP, 1985-2021)
abstract: Question: bird communities and species on North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) routes follow only a small part of their spatial temperature associations in time. Is this weak space-for-time transfer specific to climate, and does land-cover change hold the community temperature index (CTI) back? Data: BBS 2026 release (69,243 standard runs, 2,986 contiguous-US routes, 1985-2021), USGS LCMAP v1.3 annual land cover in 400 m buffers of 3,229 route paths, NOAA nClimGrid May-July climate. Method: for 384 species, cross-fitted spatial Poisson models of route abundance on temperature, precipitation and land-cover fractions gave predicted log abundance for each run from that year's land cover and 5-year climate; conditional Poisson panels with route x observer and year effects gave the temporal response per unit of spatial prediction (theta; 1 = full transfer). Split-fold reliability corrected for errors in the spatial coefficients. We decomposed the CTI trend with spatial and within-route models and a 4-degree block bootstrap. Results: theta was 0.106 (95% CI 0.064-0.148) for land cover and 0.050 (0.040-0.060) for temperature. After the reliability correction it was 0.19 (0.11-0.27) and 0.090 (0.067-0.115); with route effects only, 0.25 and 0.12. Temperature transfer was 0.47 (0.29-0.83) of land-cover transfer. Land cover 5 years before the survey also predicted counts (0.099), but land cover 5 years after did not (placebo 0.033, -0.004 to 0.071). Routes with large land-cover change gave lower theta (0.077), so classification noise does not explain the result. Land-cover change was small and implied a CTI change of +0.0020 C per decade (0.0007-0.0036); it increased the gap between the spatial climate expectation (0.096) and the observed within-observer CTI trend (0.034) by 3%. Natural-cover share, land-cover diversity and land-cover change did not modify the CTI trend. Conclusion: species follow even a direct habitat driver at only a small fraction of the spatial prediction, so most of the weak climate tracking is a general space-for-time gap; the climate-specific part is about a factor of two. Land-cover class change is not the missing process. Limitations: eight broad LCMAP classes miss forest age and agricultural intensity; 1998 route paths; 120-240 m overviews and 13 sampled years; the reliability correction assumes classical errors; checks after the main estimate are post hoc.
